body_markdown:
No vehicle is more synonymous with *La Dolce Vita* than the Vespa motor scooter. Enduring images of Marcello Mastroianni riding through Rome in Fellini’s 1960 cinematic masterpiece cemented the Vespa’s place in popular culture. Even today, no trip to Italy is complete without the experience of being buzzed by a Vespa rider, and you’ll capitalize on the fun by renting one and seeing the sights like a local.


There’s a real romance to riding a Vespa, especially two-up, with your partner clinging to your waist as you carve around the Colosseum or wend your way along the Amalfi Coast. Even if you’re simply using it to commute, you can easily entertain yourself with such thoughts.


Affairs of the heart could not have been further from the thoughts of the[Piaggio](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/piaggio-celebrates-140-years-with-a-special-edition-vespa/) family when the first Vespa was built 80 years ago. Industrialist Rinaldo Piaggio had made his fortune in fitting out ships, trucks, and trains before moving into aviation during World War I. When hostilities commenced once again, Piaggio was one of the largest aircraft manufacturers in Italy. Consequently, the company’s factories were targeted by Allied bombers during World War II. By the end of the war, there was much rebuilding to do.


Rinaldo’s son Enrico was put in charge of the facility at Pontedera and turned his attention back to ground-level transportation. Italy was impoverished and in ruins. What was needed to get the country moving again, he believed, was inexpensive transportation for the masses.


Enrico Piaggio at the Vespa factory in 1956


Vespa


The first prototype was a 98cc scooter designed in 1945 by Renzo Spolti. Those who assembled it nicknamed it *Paperino* , Italian for Donald Duck. Piaggio was not impressed. Only around 100 examples were built before Corradino D’Ascanio was tasked with replacing it.


The brief was for a robust, stylish, cheap two-wheeler that anyone could ride without sullying their clothes. D’Ascanio’s background was in aeronautics, and he drew on that experience when designing Paperino’s successor. The front suspension was modeled on the landing gear of an aircraft, the two-stroke, single-cylinder engine and transmission were mounted directly to the rear wheel, and the gear selector was located on the handlebar.


Enrico Piaggio was sold. The scooter needed only a name, which came to him the moment he saw it. “It looks like a wasp,” he said. The Italian word for wasp, of course, is *vespa* .


A production version was ready by April 1946. The Vespa 98 was unveiled to the public at the golf club in Rome. The scooter sported a new Piaggio logo and an improved top speed of almost 40 mph. Priced at 55,000 Lira, the little wasp soon took flight, and almost 2500 were built in the first year.


In the 80 years since, Vespa has developed more than 160 different models. One million units had shipped within its first decade, and, at the time of writing, the total tops 20 million.


[As it enters its ninth decade](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/vespas-will-swarm-the-circuit-at-the-2026-goodwood-revival/) , Vespa is still Italian-owned, with the Piaggio, Aprilia, and Moto Guzzi brands all under the same corporate roof, and Vespa delivering the lion’s share of global sales.


Adored by artists, engineers, commuters, and young lovers alike, Vespa continues to live *La Dolce Vita* . Here are 13 examples that chart its trajectory from the 1940s to now.


## 1945 Piaggio MP5 Paperino


Vespa


The Vespa’s journey began with Spolti’s Paperino, but neither the aesthetics nor the engineering were a hit with Enrico Piaggio. With just 100 or so built, surviving examples are potentially worth six figures.


## 1945 Piaggio MP6


Vespa


D’Ascanio’s prototype was the machine that gave the Vespa its name, after Piaggio likened its looks to a wasp.


## 1946 Vespa 98


Vespa


The first production Vespa was initially sold through the Lancia dealer network. A luxury version was available for 66,000 Lira. In 2016 an early example sold for 230,000 Euros, equivalent to around $265,000.


## 1949 Vespa 125


Vespa


Expanding the engine’s displacement to 125cc gave the Vespa a top speed in excess of 40 mph and opened up export markets. There were also updates to the front and rear suspension for increased comfort and improved handling.


## 1955 Vespa 150 Sidecar


Vespa


For almost a decade passengers had to perch behind the rider, but in 1955, Vespa offered a different solution. The new 150 could be specified with a sidecar, which was fitted with coil spring suspension and linked to the scooter by a single tube. Apparently it won much praise for its handling in the snow.


## 1956 Vespa 150 TAP


Vespa


Taking inspiration from America’s Cushman Airborne scooter, the French military decided that the Vespa 150 had the potential to be armed and deployed by parachute. The *Truppe Aero Portate* (Air Troup Carrier) was built by Piaggo France and featured a 75mm cannon. Around 600 were built and deployed by the French Foreign Legion.


## 1962 Vespa Dalì


Vespa


In 1962 Santiago Guillen and Antonio Veciana took a holiday from Madrid University to explore Europe on their Spanish-built Vespa 150. They met Salvador Dalí in Cadaqués, Spain. The artist proceeded to paint their bike, creating the world’s most valuable Vespa in the process.


## 1963 Vespa 50 N


Vespa


The Vespa 50 targeted Italy’s youth. Riders as young as 14 could ride the 50cc bike at speeds of up to 25 mph. The last Vespa to be designed by Corradino D’Ascanio, the 50 series has proved to be the most popular in Vespa’s history, with more than three million made.


## 1964 180 Super Sport


Vespa


The 180 Super Sport of 1964 occupied the other end of the Vespa performance spectrum, with engine displacement pushed up to 180 cc and a top speed of over 100 km/h (a Vespa first). Given enough space, the 180 could actually reach 65 mph.


## 1985 Vespa 125 PX T5


Dietmar / Wikimedia Commons


The PX stood for Pole Position, and Vespa played on its racing connection with its most potent 125 to date. It was powered by a new five-port two-cylinder engine and endorsed by F1 champion Nelson Piquet.


## 1991 50 Special Revival


Vespa


A throwback to the Swinging Sixties, the 50 Special was limited to a run of just 3000, but its stylish retro design was enough to win it a place at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.


### 2015 946 Emporio Armani


Vespa


Riding a Vespa has always been a fashion statement, and in 2015 came a tie-up to make it official. Marking the 130th anniversary of the Piaggio Group and 40 years of Giorgio Armani’s business was the 946 Emporio Armani, finished in unique color-shifting paintwork with galvanized metal trim.


## 2026 Vespa *Edizione Ottantesimo*


Vespa


To celebrate its 80th anniversary, Vespa introduced the *Edizione Ottantesimo,* based on the[GTS 310](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2025-vespa-gts-310-pictures-specs/) . Exactly 1946 examples are to be built, with 25 designated for the U.S.A.
